title: Flip the condition, swap the branches
idea: Many if/else problems can be written two ways by flipping the condition and swapping the branches. Understanding this deepens the model. Thinking-heavy.

exercises.prompt:
These two do the same thing. True or false - they give the same outputs?

A: if n > 0:
    print("pos")
else:
    print("not pos")

B: if n <= 0:
    print("not pos")
else:
    print("pos")
exercises.explanation: Flipping > 0 to <= 0 and swapping the branches gives identical behavior. Both label positives 'pos'.

exercises.prompt: The opposite of the condition n > 0 is...
exercises.explanation: The opposite of 'greater than 0' is 'less than OR equal to 0': n <= 0. The equal case flips sides.

exercises.prompt: Match each condition to its opposite.
exercises.explanation: Flipping a condition swaps the boundary case too: >= becomes <, > becomes <=, == becomes !=.
'50 or more' flips to 'less than 50': score < 50. Watch the boundary - 50 itself now falls on the other side.

options: if not-paid: print "Please pay" else print "Thanks"
if paid: print "Please pay" else print "Thanks"
exercises.explanation: Flip the condition to the False case and swap the two messages - the behavior stays the same.

exercises.prompt: If you flip the condition but forget to swap the branches, the behavior changes.
exercises.explanation: Yes - flipping the condition alone reverses which message each case gets. You must swap the branches too.
'Equal to 5' flips to 'not equal to 5': n != 5.

exercises.prompt: Why might you prefer one wording over the other?
options: To put the more common or clearer case in the if branch
exercises.explanation: Both work, so you choose the version that reads more clearly - often the common case in the if.

exercises.prompt:
Write the opposite of n < 10:

n ____ 10
exercises.explanation: The opposite of 'less than 10' is 'greater than or equal to 10': n >= 10. The boundary 10 switches sides.

exercises.prompt: What is the big idea of this lesson?
options: A two-way choice can be written two equivalent ways by flipping and swapping
exercises.explanation: Seeing that if/else can be flipped shows you understand the choice, not just the syntax.
